scenes.tts: How can a bat wing and a protein point to the same relatives? The first film used fossils to track change through time. Now we will test relationships among the branches.
scenes.caption: How can a bat wing and a protein point to the same relatives? The first film used fossils to track change through time. Now we will test relationships among the branches.
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's sixteen-by-nine riverbank without resetting the world. Reuse its COLOUR MAP exactly: fossils GOLD; matching body structures BLUE; DNA and protein sequences TEAL; supported inferences GREEN; missing or uncertain evidence GRAY. The riverbank and GOLD fossils slide left while the unresolved GRAY family branches from the first film grow to fill sixty percent of the frame. A BLUE bone-block icon and TEAL protein strip hover beside them. Text asks 'Which branches are closest?' Ambient water and drifting grains continue.
scenes.narration: How can a bat wing and a protein point to the same relatives? The first film used fossils to track change through time. Now we will test relationships among the branches.

scenes.visual: Title 'Two Clues, One Family Tree' appears above the carried gray branches for two seconds. The blue bone block rotates gently, teal sequence marks drift into alignment, and the river keeps moving at the left edge.

scenes.tts: A common ancestor is an earlier population from which later groups came. Picture one branch splitting. Each new branch inherits old features, then changes in its own direction.
scenes.caption: A common ancestor is an earlier population from which later groups came. Picture one branch splitting. Each new branch inherits old features, then changes in its own direction.
scenes.visual: Center one thick GRAY trunk. It grows upward, then divides into several branches. At the split, a GREEN circle labelled 'common ancestor' appears. Identical BLUE blocks ride into every new branch. As branches lengthen, the blocks stretch into different outlines while keeping their order. A small 'schematic' label remains at bottom right through the film.
scenes.narration: A common ancestor is an earlier population from which later groups came. Picture one branch splitting. Each new branch inherits old features, then changes in its own direction.

scenes.tts: A human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing have an upper bone and paired lower bones. Wrist and finger bones follow. Shapes and jobs differ, but positions match.
scenes.caption: A human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing have an upper bone and paired lower bones. Wrist and finger bones follow. Shapes and jobs differ, but positions match.
scenes.visual: The BLUE blocks expand into four large simplified limb diagrams made from labelled blocks. Keep the same shade for corresponding parts. Place the human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing across the branches. As each part is named, a blue guide line sweeps across all four corresponding positions. The outlines reshape for different jobs while the block order stays fixed.
scenes.narration: A human arm, cat leg, whale flipper, and bat wing have an upper bone and paired lower bones. Wrist and finger bones follow. Shapes and jobs differ, but positions match.

scenes.tts: Scientists compare construction and position, not only jobs. Inherited changes can reshape an old set of parts. That shared bone map points back toward a common ancestor.
scenes.caption: Scientists compare construction and position, not only jobs. Inherited changes can reshape an old set of parts. That shared bone map points back toward a common ancestor.
scenes.visual: Job labels 'grasp', 'walk', 'swim', and 'fly' move away from the limbs. The BLUE bone blocks stay. Matching-position lines fold inward and attach to the same GREEN ancestor circle. A gray tag reading 'same job?' drifts aside, while a green tag reading 'same construction and position' locks beside the shared branch.
scenes.narration: Scientists compare construction and position, not only jobs. Inherited changes can reshape an old set of parts. That shared bone map points back toward a common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Sequences offer a test. A D N A sequence is the order of its bases. Many genes carry instructions for proteins. Scientists can line up the same protein from several species, position by position.
scenes.caption: Sequences offer a test. A DNA sequence is the order of its bases. Many genes carry instructions for proteins. Scientists can line up the same protein from several species, position by position.
scenes.visual: Shrink the limbs but keep them attached to the branches. TEAL letter strips labelled 'DNA sequence' enter, then transform into simple TEAL protein strips made of equal labelled blocks, without molecular structures. Several species' strips stack and align at the left edge. A vertical cursor moves across them position by position, highlighting matches and marking differences with pale teal ticks.
scenes.narration: Sequences offer a test. A DNA sequence is the order of its bases. Many genes carry instructions for proteins. Scientists can line up the same protein from several species, position by position.

scenes.tts: Some inherited D N A changes remain in later populations. Branches split at different times, so closer relatives usually have more similar sequences. Usually matters. Changes do not build up at one steady rate.
scenes.caption: Some inherited DNA changes remain in later populations. Branches split at different times, so closer relatives usually have more similar sequences. Usually matters. Changes do not build up at one steady rate.
scenes.visual: Run a schematic clock while two nearby branches and one earlier branch lengthen. TEAL difference ticks appear occasionally along each branch, at visibly uneven intervals. The nearby pair's aligned strips share more positions; the earlier branch carries more ticks. Keep 'schematic' beside the clock. On 'Usually matters', the clock wobbles and a fixed-rate ruler fades out.
scenes.narration: Some inherited DNA changes remain in later populations. Branches split at different times, so closer relatives usually have more similar sequences. Usually matters. Changes do not build up at one steady rate.

scenes.tts: Now test two clues. Species ay and bee share a blue structure that see lacks. A teal protein strip joins ay with see. Have the clues agreed, and should any branch turn green yet?
scenes.caption: Now test two clues. Species A and B share a blue structure that C lacks. A teal protein strip joins A with C. Have the clues agreed, and should any branch turn green yet?
scenes.visual: Use neutral labels 'species A', 'species B', and 'species C' on three large GRAY branches. A BLUE bracket labelled 'shared structure, C lacks it' joins A and B. A TEAL bracket joins A and C. No branch is green. Large white question text appears: 'Do the clues agree?' All moving ticks and blocks slow, but continue a faint drift.
scenes.narration: Now test two clues. Species A and B share a blue structure that C lacks. A teal protein strip joins A with C. Have the clues agreed, and should any branch turn green yet?

scenes.visual: Deliberate prediction pause. Hold both conflicting brackets and the question. The gray branches sway almost imperceptibly; blue blocks and teal ticks shimmer faintly.

scenes.tts: No. The clues support different groupings. Keep the branches gray, check the comparison, and collect more evidence. A conflict is not something to hide. It is a question to investigate.
scenes.caption: No. The clues support different groupings. Keep the branches gray, check the comparison, and collect more evidence. A conflict is not something to hide. It is a question to investigate.
scenes.visual: The question becomes 'Not yet'. Both brackets stay visible, but the family branches remain GRAY. A magnifying glass passes over the bone positions and sequence alignment. Additional empty evidence slots appear around the branches. A large gray question mark settles above the split without any final-status label.
scenes.narration: No. The clues support different groupings. Keep the branches gray, check the comparison, and collect more evidence. A conflict is not something to hide. It is a question to investigate.

scenes.tts: Now a different case. Two species share a structure that a third species lacks. The protein strip groups that same pair. When independent clues agree, their shared branch is the stronger explanation.
scenes.caption: Now a different case. Two species share a structure that a third species lacks. The protein strip groups that same pair. When independent clues agree, their shared branch is the stronger explanation.
scenes.visual: A separate panel labelled 'a different case' slides in with three new GRAY branches, species D, E and F; the earlier conflict stays gray at the edge. A BLUE bracket labelled 'shared structure, F lacks it' and a TEAL bracket both join D and E. As the narration reaches 'that same pair', their shared branch changes from GRAY to GREEN. The two brackets merge into a single green outline around D and E. The other branch stays gray without receiving a final label.
scenes.narration: Now a different case. Two species share a structure that a third species lacks. The protein strip groups that same pair. When independent clues agree, their shared branch is the stronger explanation.

scenes.tts: This is how a scientific theory earns trust. Each line of evidence could have told a different story. Evolution predicts broad agreement among fossils, structures, and sequences. Their broad patterns largely agree.
scenes.caption: This is how a scientific theory earns trust. Each line of evidence could have told a different story. Evolution predicts broad agreement among fossils, structures, and sequences. Their broad patterns largely agree.
scenes.visual: Bring back the GOLD fossil layer at left, BLUE limb map at center, and TEAL aligned strips at right. Each sends a moving line toward the carried family tree. A central GREEN label reads 'evolution: tested explanation'. A new blank evidence card slides in, and a question-mark arrow from the explanation reaches toward it to show a testable prediction.
scenes.narration: This is how a scientific theory earns trust. Each line of evidence could have told a different story. Evolution predicts broad agreement among fossils, structures, and sequences. Their broad patterns largely agree.

scenes.tts: One limb or one small protein cannot settle every relationship. Similar jobs can evolve in different structures. Scientists compare more body parts, more sequences, and the fossil record.
scenes.caption: One limb or one small protein cannot settle every relationship. Similar jobs can evolve in different structures. Scientists compare more body parts, more sequences, and the fossil record.
scenes.visual: The single blue limb and single teal strip become small cards labelled 'one clue'. GRAY uncertainty frames surround them. They transform into three large stacked decks: BLUE 'more body parts', TEAL 'more sequences', and GOLD 'fossil record'. The gray frames shrink but do not vanish. Keep every graph or rate display absent; this is a schematic comparison.
scenes.narration: One limb or one small protein cannot settle every relationship. Similar jobs can evolve in different structures. Scientists compare more body parts, more sequences, and the fossil record.

scenes.tts: Return to the family tree. Matching parts show inherited construction. Similar sequences in the same protein add an independent check. When both fit one branch pattern, common ancestry explains the match best.
scenes.caption: Return to the family tree. Matching parts show inherited construction. Similar sequences in the same protein add an independent check. When both fit one branch pattern, common ancestry explains the match best.
scenes.visual: Rebuild the complete carried family tree. BLUE limb blocks travel backward along two branches toward one GREEN ancestor circle. TEAL protein strips align above those same branches, and their matching positions glow. The blue and teal guide lines meet at the same green split. GOLD fossils remain along the time base, linking this film's relationship test to the first film's history.
scenes.narration: Return to the family tree. Matching parts show inherited construction. Similar sequences in the same protein add an independent check. When both fit one branch pattern, common ancestry explains the match best.

scenes.tts: The clues do different jobs. Fossils place life in time. Bones of living and fossil animals, plus sequences, test relationships. Their broad agreement supports evolution, while every uncertainty stays visible and open to testing.
scenes.caption: The clues do different jobs. Fossils place life in time. Bones of living and fossil animals, plus sequences, test relationships. Their broad agreement supports evolution, while every uncertainty stays visible and open to testing.
scenes.visual: Arrange three large carried panels around the tree: GOLD 'time', BLUE 'structure', and TEAL 'sequence'. Each panel connects to the parts of the tree it can support. GREEN highlights broad agreement. Small GRAY question marks remain at unresolved splits and gently pulse. The scene dims without adding a teaser or new claim.
scenes.narration: The clues do different jobs. Fossils place life in time. Bones of living and fossil animals, plus sequences, test relationships. Their broad agreement supports evolution, while every uncertainty stays visible and open to testing.

scenes.visual: One-line end card over the dimmed family tree. Large centered white text: 'Matching structures and protein sequences point to common ancestry.' No smaller line. Blue bone blocks and teal sequence ticks drift slowly behind it while the supported branch remains green.
